Concise Clinical Note

Consult Summary:
50-year-old man with 4–5 day history of cough, rhinorrhoea, sore throat, subjective fever and new mild shortness of breath; clinical impression most consistent with an acute viral upper-respiratory/ influenza-like illness. Safety-net (“delayed”) antibiotic script provided in case of progression.

History:
• Presenting symptoms: Felt “run-down” since Saturday (≈5 days). Dry cough (occasional “mucky” phlegm, worse mornings), runny nose/sniffles, sore throat, mild ear dullness, subjective fevers with night sweats/chills, general myalgias/joint stiffness, one day of diarrhoea now resolved, mild shortness of breath without chest pain.  
• Pertinent negatives: No vomiting, no chest pain, no significant ear pain, appetite preserved.  
• Past medical history: Type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, overweight/obesity.  
• Medications: Metformin, Lisinopril; intermittent aspirin.  
• Allergies: No known drug allergies.  
• Social / preventive: Lives with wife, children moved out. Factory worker (steel parts). Alcohol ≈9 pints beer/week. Occasional smoker—transitioning to vaping. No recent travel or known sick contacts reported. Vaccination status not discussed.

Examination:
( Telephone consultation – no vitals obtained )  
• Clinician noted audible nasal congestion/sniffles over phone.  
• No other physical findings documented.

Impression:
Most likely:  
1. Acute viral upper respiratory infection / influenza-like illness (incl. possible COVID-19) – fits acute onset of cough, rhinorrhoea, sore throat, myalgias, feverishness.  
Possible alternatives:  
2. Community-acquired pneumonia – moderate likelihood given purulent sputum, diabetes, increasing dyspnoea; lack of objective fever or chest findings argue against but warrants watch.  
3. Acute bronchitis – could explain sub-acute cough with minimal systemic toxicity; overlaps with viral URI.

Plan:
• Conservative measures: rest, maintain hydration, regular paracetamol/acetaminophen for fever or aches.  
• Delayed antibiotic prescription: Amoxicillin 1 tablet three times daily to be started if no improvement or worsening (especially breathlessness or fever) within 24–48 hours.  
• Red flag advice: seek urgent review for severe or persistent dyspnoea, chest pain, high fever, confusion, or if unable to maintain oral intake.  
• Follow-up: re-assessment next week if still symptomatic, or sooner if any concerns.  
• Chronic disease care: encourage smoking cessation (continuing vaping aid) and moderation of alcohol; no immediate changes to metformin/lisinopril.

Quality checks:

● Missing/expected elements: objective vitals (T°, BP, HR, RR, SpO₂); physical chest/airway examination; vaccination history (influenza, COVID); documentation of dose/duration for amoxicillin; explicit follow-up date.  
● Conflicts: Transcript describes mainly dry cough but also admits “mucky phlegm” – minor inconsistency; otherwise DDx aligns with transcript.  
● Transcript quality: Clear but telephone format limits exam; some colloquial language; overall adequate history but objective data sparse.
